pitchfork.title: Late Loop
pitchfork.description: Featuring heartbroken vocal performances and stripped of frills like basslines or reverb, the Manchester producer’s latest album of bruised electronica is his starkest and most forlorn yet.

pitchfork.title: The Girl of Your Dreams
pitchfork.description: The “Stop the Wedding!” singer’s vintage-styled new album combines stately pop classicism and exuberant ’70s pastiche.

pitchfork.title: Passing the Cup of Sorrows
pitchfork.description: The Disintegration Loops made the composer’s name synonymous with weighty meditations on memory and loss, but his latest album—calm, focused, tender—is a reminder of his fondness for beauty.

pitchfork.title: Everything in Readiness
pitchfork.description: Marrying lush arrangements and field-recording experiments, the English revivalists honor folk music’s radical tradition by reinforcing its contemporary significance.

pitchfork.title: Katamari Fortissimo Damacy
pitchfork.description: Each Sunday, Pitchfork takes an in-depth look at a significant album from the past, and any record not in our archives is eligible. Today, we reconnect with a 2004 cult-classic game whose postmodernist soundtrack doubles as a treatise on the meaning of life.

pitchfork.title: Drukqs (25th Anniversary Edition)
pitchfork.description: Richard D. James’ once divisive 2001 album today looks, with 25 years of hindsight, like the keystone of his career, joining rave mischief and academic rigor in a sprawling, 100-minute package.

pitchfork.title: ZIRP!
pitchfork.description: The shoegaze band teams with producer A. G. Cook for its most pop-leaning record yet. Despite some welcome shifts in tone, the best moments sound like no one but DIIV.

pitchfork.title: Awesome
pitchfork.description: Upstart guitarist Heath Michael Thomas’ shaggy, groove-heavy garage rock captures the raucous interplay of a much more practiced band.

quietus.title: Remember Them: The Incalculable Legacy of Juan Atkins
quietus.description: Alex Maiolo salutes a visionary musician – "The Originator" of techno – who died on Saturday night Juan Atkins was born in Detroit, Michigan in 1962. His parents split when he was a teen. The plan was for him and his father to move to California, but his grandparents made the case for them to take up residence down the street in the Detroit suburb of Belleville. This was only the first time Juan’s grandmother, Lily, had a direct effect on the history of electronic music.The second was when she helped the 15-year-old buy a monosynth. Already playing in funk bands, Atkins took note of Bernie Worrell’s work in Funkadelic. Apparently Lily could absolutely tear it up on the Hammond B3...

quietus.title: A Form of Utopianism: Cluster’s Sowiesoso at 50
quietus.description: From avant garde beginnings to ambient endings, Cluster reconfigured rock music as much as Kraftwerk, says Toby Manning. In the late 70s and early 80s, British music took a distinctly European turn, from Bowie’s “Heroes” in 1977 to Ultravox’s ‘Vienna’ in 1981, peaking with Kraftwerk’s ‘The Model’ hitting UK no. 1 the following year. Whether it was the after-effects of the EEC referendum or a growing anti-Americanism in the wake of Watergate and Vietnam, this new Europeanism temporarily sidelined music’s traditional Transatlantic passage for the artier terrain over the Channel. Chart hits like Visage’s ‘Fade To Grey’ in 1980, The Passions’ 1981 ‘I’m In Love With A German Film Star’, or The…

quietus.title: How Pete Doherty’s Mega-Breakfast Predicted GB Music Radio
quietus.description: Pete Paphides reaches for the Gaviscon as he considers national identity, large plates of fried food, and what would be on the playlist were he celebrating British culture on the airwaves Pete Doherty eating his breakfast at the Dalby Cafe, via Instagram It’s been ten years since, over a Muswell Hill cuppa, my pop-loving compañero Bob Stanley floated a theory that was, on the face of things, a mite fanciful. He suggested that a key factor in the outcome of the 2016 referendum on leaving the EU was the similarity between the words ‘Brexit’ and ‘breakfast’. Bob contended that those of us who wanted Britain to remain in the EU didn’t have a comparably snappy word to which we could align our...

quietus.title: Subscriber Exclusive Playlist & Perks Round-up: October 2026
quietus.description: Here's everything our Subscribers had last month, including over four hours of listening treasure in the multi-platform playlist It’s that time of the month when we take the heavy lifting from our Subscribers' ears and keep them on top of all that is new and good in tQ’s world. Before we give the Subscriber and Subscriber Plus tier members the links to their playlist on the various streaming platforms, here’s a bit of a catch-up on what we’ve sent out to our top two subs tiers in October. In the Low Culture Podcast, John and Luke discussed the original 1954 film that kicked off the Godzilla series, as well as the recent Godzilla Minus One. The Low Culture Essay was on...

quietus.title: The Last Path – Blunt Synopsis
quietus.description: The Last Path Blunt Synopsis Formerly known as Bad Amputee, trio from the north-east of England take things slow. Real slow Blunt Synopsis by The Last Path When the sort of music The Last Path play really lands, the secret to it doing so is in how it just teeters on the absolute precipice of unsalvageable dourness. Guitars that sound innately metallic, not as in the genre but evocative of a large amount of lead ingots plummeting from the sky onto rural limestone. Vocals that draw out nigh on every vowel sound, not for melismatic or otherwise showy reasons but just to figuratively look you in the eye and say, “I’ll finish singing this line when I’m ready, thanks”. Blunt Synopsis is the…

quietus.title: Sacrificial Riffology: Reconsidering Altar by Boris & Sunn O)))
quietus.description: Where do you go, what do you do, after you have created a riff for the ages? For Keith Kahn-Harris, that's the question that Boris & Sunn O)))'s Altar seems to ask By any objective standard, the riff that dominates 'Etna', the opener to the Boris / Sunn O))) collaboration Altar, should be as celebrated as 'Walk', 'Whole Lotta Love' or 'Symptom Of The Universe'. As a song, there is little else to it but the riff – an extended intro that builds and locks into an audaciously simple chord sequence, eventually giving way to a lavishly elongated breakdown into a squall of guitar noise. It's 9 minutes and 50 seconds of metallic perfection, the apotheosis of focused guitar power, without...

quietus.title: Enemies Within: Derek Jarman’s Kicking the Pricks and The Last of England
quietus.description: Republished for the first time in nearly thirty years, Derek Jarman's book Kicking the Pricks, including the director's notes and diaries from the making of his seminal film The Last of England, offers a portal into a rotting UK that feels all too familiar The Last of England (Derek Jarman, 1987). All images courtesy: British Film Institute In Kicking The Pricks Derek Jarman poses the question: what use is a film, book or artwork that presents a nostalgic future warning for an unloved and thwarted isle? A companion piece to Jarman’s most overtly political film, The Last Of England, the book is part memoir, part production diary, and a scattering of interviews. Taken together, the two works…

quietus.title: Gutted, Hashed and Deboned: Necroticism: Descanting the Insalubrious By Carcass At 35
quietus.description: Keith Kahn-Harris looks back at a landmark release full of surprises and possibilities To push back a genre label is, all too often, a reliably generic move by artists desperately seeking to differentiate themselves from other artists who sound much the same. Occasionally though, pushing back against genre label is a more subversive move, the mark of an artist pushing against anything that would close off their creative development. Such is the case with Carcass. It didn’t take them long at the start of their career to reject the grindcore label, they are currently rebelling against the extreme metal label, and on Necroticism: Descanting The Insalubrious they were reluctant to be labelled…

aquariumdrunkard.title: Chrome Chasm :: The Aquarium Drunkard Interview
aquariumdrunkard.description: The Houston-based trio known as Chrome Chasm features three veteran improvisers doing what they do best — improvising. Together, guitarist Tom Carter (Charalambides), saxophonist/flautist Mlee Marie (Hearts of Animals) and pedal steel-er Will Adams (Lower Dens, Ka-Nives) create bewitching, twilit music that’s somehow both minimalist and wide-open — a vast landscape that somehow contains countless sonic details. Aquarium Drunkard chatted with Tom, Mlee and Will to find out more.

aquariumdrunkard.title: Miles Davis: Europe ‘71
aquariumdrunkard.description: Across the Miles Davis electric era there’s no greater divide than that between 1972’s On the Corner and what came before it. But the signposts are there if you know where to look, with recordings from a European tour in the fall of ‘71 revealing Miles subtly, deftly moving the pieces into place for his next iteration.

aquariumdrunkard.title: Jason Dungan & Johan Carøe :: Routine
aquariumdrunkard.description: Copenhagen-based composers Jason Dungan (Blue Lake) and Johan Carøe join forces on Routine , a quietly transportive collection of ambient folk and new age soundscapes shaped through an exchange of musical fragments. Blending acoustic instrumentation, electronics, and Dungan’s self-designed 36-string zither, the duo arrive at something intimate and unhurried—a luminous meditation on domestic ritual, the rhythms of everyday life, and the quiet wonder of being alive.

aquariumdrunkard.title: Panamint :: S/T
aquariumdrunkard.description: Panamint began as a studio experiment between longtime collaborators Anna St. Louis and producer Jarvis Taveniere, who reunited to put Taveniere’s new Los Angeles studio through its paces. What started with left-field covers of Post Malone and Helene Smith soon evolved into a set of original recordings, joined by Danny Garcia, aka Reverend Baron. Out this week, their self-titled debut EP draws on the timeless pull of vintage soul and classic pop.

aquariumdrunkard.title: Sam Gendel :: Advanced White Trash
aquariumdrunkard.description: In his classic book Mythologies, French thinker Roland Barthes criticizes plastic because it can be molded into anything—cheap, colorful surfaces open to infinite transformation. Contemporary pop is made of the same stuff, and Sam Gendel’s Advanced White Trash makes the case for what’s beautiful, even freeing, about it. The record sounds like something that was uploaded to SoundCloud at 3 a.m., a Roland Sound Canvas emulator buffering on a dying phone someone found in a Walmart parking lot, and still it comes out strangely appealing, almost hypnotic.

aquariumdrunkard.title: Ana Palindrome :: A MAN A CURE
aquariumdrunkard.description: Cork trio Ana Palindrome make a hypnotic blend of art-pop, droning vocals, sawing fiddle, and glitchy folktronica on “A MAN A CURE,” their first release for London’s World of Echo. Beneath its pulsing rhythms and woozy electronics, the track questions the idea of self-made identity, as Niamh Dalton’s voice shifts between the organic and the artificial.

aquariumdrunkard.title: Boards of Canada :: Hi Scores
aquariumdrunkard.description: Earlier this year, Boards of Canada unexpectedly released their fifth album Inferno , a case of an influential artist demonstrating that their style remains eminently relatable in 2026 a.d. To close out the year, the group has dipped into its archives, re-releasing the 1996 EP Hi Scores . There’s plenty to savor here, especially for longtime BOC listeners, but there’s also something compelling about being able to hear the group’s roots in such close temporal proximity to their current venture.

mubi.description: One Sings, the Other Doesn't (Agnès Varda, 1977). In her memoir, Varda par Agnès , the French director describes herself as “une féministe de terrain plus qu’une discuteuse,” roughly translated as “a feminist on the ground rather than in theory.” Later in the book, she describes the “feminists” discussing her work, implying that she was outside this group. How feminist she reads from any angle now is unclear. Many would, for instance, find her focus on the body and childbirth essentialist. Her 1975 short, Réponse de femmes: Notre corps, notre sexe ( Women Reply: Our Bodies, Our Sex ), opens with this prompt: “What does it mean to be a woman?” The text is painted on glass and held up by two…

A few months earlier, the same film had world premiered at Cannes, in the Un Certain Regard section, and walked away with a special mention for the Caméra d’Or. It was the first Nigerian film to be programmed in the official selection at the festival. Variety called Akinola Davies Jr.’s film miraculous. Rotten Tomatoes aggregated the critical assessment as 98% positive. However, there exists a cultural invisibility at home that stands against these genuine international recognitions.
